title: Comparison of pre- versus post-incisional trocar-site infiltration with long-acting local anesthetics for reducing postoperative pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair: a randomized controlled trial
summary:
After laparoscopic removal of the gallbladder, patients may experience pain at the sites where surgical instruments pass through the abdominal wall. One method to reduce this pain is the injection of a long-acting local anesthetic at these sites.

It is assumed that infiltration before skin incision may reduce pain caused by the passage of instruments through the muscle layers and fascia. Whether this early infiltration results in less pain compared with infiltration at the end of surgery has not yet been clearly established.

In this study, patients undergoing laparoscopic gallbladder removal or inguinal hernia repair will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. After surgery, analgesic consumption will be assessed first, followed by pain intensity at several time points. The aim is to minimize the use of strong analgesics while ensuring effective pain control.
conditions: Postoperative pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, with particular focus on pain at abdominal wall trocar insertion sites.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age ≥ 18 years
Scheduled elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy or inguinal hernia repair
Ability to understand the study procedures and provide written informed consent
ASA physical status I–III
Procedure performed using a standard Muli-port laparoscopic technique
Exclusion criteria:
Known allergy or hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics (e.g., ropivacaine)
Chronic pain syndromes or regular preoperative opioid use
Acute cholecystitis or emergency surgery
Conversion to open cholecystectomy
Previous upper abdominal surgery with significant scarring
Severe hepatic or renal impairment
Pregnancy or breastfeeding
